name: Ariadne
summary: A schema-first Python GraphQL library: you write the schema in SDL and bind plain Python functions to its fields.
intro: In Ariadne the schema is text. You write it in GraphQL’s Schema Definition Language (SDL), as a Python string or in `.graphql` files, and optionally wrap it in `gql()` so a syntax error points at your schema rather than at Ariadne’s internals. Resolvers are plain functions. You attach them with bindables: a `QueryType` or `ObjectType("Book")` object whose `@query.field("book")` decorator names the field a function resolves. `make_executable_schema(type_defs, query, book)` parses the SDL into a GraphQL-core schema and binds each function to its field, raising `ValueError` if a bindable names a type or field the schema doesn’t define. A field with no bound resolver falls back to GraphQL-core’s default resolver, which reads the key or attribute of the same name from the parent object. A resolver gets the parent object, an `info` object whose `context` holds the request, and the field’s arguments as keyword arguments; `convert_names_case=True` maps camelCase names in the schema to snake_case in Python.

`ariadne.asgi.GraphQL` is an ASGI application, built on Starlette, that serves queries over HTTP and subscriptions over WebSockets, with a GraphiQL explorer built in; a WSGI version exists too. In FastAPI you either mount it as a sub-application or call its `handle_request()` from your own routes, which lets FastAPI dependencies such as a database session reach the GraphQL context. Mirumee, a software company, created it in 2018 and kept it on 0.x versions until 1.0.0 in March 2026; it follows SemVer since. Version 1.1.0 (June 2026) added an automated SQLAlchemy integration, and 1.1.1 (October 7, 2026) added support for GraphQL-core 3.3.
strengths: The SDL is the contract: frontend and backend developers read and review the same schema, and GraphQL tools work on it directly
Small API of plain functions and bindables, with no global registry, so one codebase can serve several GraphQL APIs
ASGI and WSGI servers, subscriptions, file uploads, Apollo Federation and integrations for Django, FastAPI, Flask and Starlette
Bindables are checked at startup: binding a resolver to a type or field the schema lacks raises an error
limits: Two sources of truth: the schema is SDL and the code is Python, connected by field names in strings. A field you forget to bind silently uses the default resolver and returns `null` if the parent has no matching key or attribute
The SDL’s camelCase meets Python’s snake_case; conversion is opt-in with `convert_names_case`
In FastAPI it runs as a mounted ASGI app, so using FastAPI dependencies means writing the GET, POST and WebSocket routes by hand

snippet.title: The same book query, schema first: SDL plus a bound resolver
source: from ariadne import QueryType, graphql_sync, make_executable_schema
# A dict is fine: the default resolver reads book["title"]
success, result = graphql_sync(schema, {"query": "{ book { title author } }"})

story: In 2018 the main Python option for GraphQL was Graphene, which builds the schema from Python classes. Mirumee wanted the schema-first style of the JavaScript server Apollo Server, where the SDL is written by hand and resolvers are attached to it. It released Ariadne 0.1.0 in October 2018, “inspired by Apollo Server and built with GraphQL-core”, after dogfooding it internally on a number of projects.

Two early changes set its shape. Version 0.2.0 (January 2019) moved to GraphQL-core-next, which supported `async` resolvers and a more recent version of the spec. Version 0.3.0 (April 2019) added an ASGI interface based on Starlette, which is how it now runs in Starlette and FastAPI. Ariadne then stayed on 0.x versions, up to 0.29, until 1.0.0 in March 2026 removed deprecated features such as Apollo tracing and OpenTracing support. Version 1.1.0 (June 2026) added an automated SQLAlchemy integration, and 1.1.1 (October 2026) supports GraphQL-core 3.3.

choices.why: The SDL is the approach most of the GraphQL community uses, and dozens of frontend and backend tools, examples and learning resources work with it. Writing the schema by hand makes all of that available to Python teams too.

choices.choice: Bindables instead of a global registry
choices.why: Resolvers attach to the schema through explicit objects passed to `make_executable_schema`, with no global state, so several GraphQL APIs can live in one codebase and reuse types explicitly.
GraphQL-core 2 didn’t support `async` resolvers or the newer spec. Switching in January 2019 gave Ariadne `async` resolvers and query execution, three months before it added an ASGI server.

timeline.text: Moves to GraphQL-core-next for `async` resolvers in January
ASGI interface built on Starlette in April
1.0.0 in March; SQLAlchemy integration in June; GraphQL-core 3.3 support in October
